Thank you, Anna Frick, for highlighting this opportunity at the World Bank Group (WBG). What makes this position or role particularly compelling is that it sits at a critical intersection between digital engineering and institutional or organizational accountability: the technology is not merely supporting an internal workflow; it underpins how development outcomes are submitted, measured, quality-assured, analysed, and ultimately communicated.
The emphasis on R or Shiny, Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), SQL, Quarto, Git, QA or UAT, and production systems also illustrates an important principle in development practice: evidence-based decision-making depends not only on having data, but on building reliable systems that transform data into credible, accessible, and actionable evidence.
I especially appreciate the connection to outcomes spanning climate, jobs, private-sector mobilisation, and development impact. Strong digital public infrastructure and robust information systems can quietly become some of the most consequential foundations of effective development institutions or organizations.
For prospective applicants, this is a valuable reminder that careers in international development increasingly extend beyond conventional policy and programme positions or roles. Data engineering, application development, digital transformation, statistical computing, and responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) are becoming integral to how global institutions or international organizations learn, measure results, and improve interventions.
